system.name: Recipe-sharing web app
system.description: Users publish recipes, browse them, comment, and upload photos. 100 registered users, 2 developers, GBP 50/month infrastructure budget, no stated availability target, no stated compliance requirements.

functional: Register, sign in, and manage an account
Publish a recipe: title, description, ingredients, steps, tags
Upload one or more photos per recipe and have web-sized derivatives generated
Browse and search recipes by title, ingredient, and tag

assumptions.text: 30% of registered users are daily active
assumptions.impact: Linear on RPS and egress. At 100% DAU every figure is 3.3x larger and the recommendation is unchanged.

assumptions.text: 2 sessions per active user per day, 40 requests per session (pages, JSON, static assets)
assumptions.impact: Linear on RPS. At 3 sessions x 60 requests the peak is 4.2 RPS, still one instance.

assumptions.text: Consumer traffic shape with evening concentration, peak factor 10 (calculators/README.md table)
assumptions.impact: Linear on peak RPS. At 20x the peak is 0.56 RPS and no provisioning decision changes.

assumptions.text: Recipes are published at 0.5 per user per month, so about 1.7 recipes/day at 100 users
assumptions.impact: Linear on database and object-storage growth. 10x is 87 GB of photos/year, about GBP 1.30-2.20/month. No decision changes.

assumptions.text: 4 photos per recipe, 2.5 MB per original upload, plus derivatives at +40% -> 3.5 MB stored per photo
assumptions.impact: Dominant term in object storage and egress. This is the input to measure first.

assumptions.text: About 20 comments/day across the site, 500 bytes per comment row
assumptions.impact: Negligible: comments contribute about 4 MB/year of database growth.

assumptions.text: Average served payload 100 KB per request, dominated by web-sized images (about 4 MB per session)
assumptions.impact: Linear on egress, which is the cost line that eventually breaks the GBP 50 budget.

assumptions.text: 5 database queries per request, 5 ms mean query time
assumptions.impact: Linear on connection demand. Even at 20 queries/request the pool is at the floor of 5.

assumptions.text: Image resize takes about 3 seconds of CPU per photo
assumptions.impact: Determines whether resizing can stay in the request path. At 6.8 photos/day it can.

assumptions.text: No compliance, residency or data-sensitivity constraints, as stated by the requester
assumptions.impact: Would change data residency, deletion, and audit requirements entirely. Note that UK/EU consumer accounts plus user-uploaded photos still carry baseline data-protection duties (deletion on request, a stated retention policy) regardless of whether a compliance programme exists.

assumptions.text: Both developers are product engineers with no dedicated operations capacity, and the team has operated a managed relational database and managed object storage before
assumptions.impact: Sets the complexity budget at 4. If either technology is unfamiliar the modifier adds 1 point and the selected architecture goes to 5/4, requiring a written override.

assumptions.text: No availability target exists because none was stated; the business tolerates hours of downtime
assumptions.impact: If 99.9% or better is actually required, database failover is needed and the infrastructure budget must rise well above GBP 50.

assumptions.text: Deployment is a single application codebase deployed as one unit on a managed platform
assumptions.impact: Each additional independently deployed service costs 1 complexity point against a budget of 4.

results.formula: requests_per_day = users x dau_share x sessions_per_day x requests_per_session; avg_rps = requests_per_day / 86400; peak_rps = avg_rps x peak_factor

safety_margin.rationale: 2x headroom on the peak factor, because an assumed traffic shape is the least reliable input in this estimate. Even the 2x figure of 0.56 RPS is three orders of magnitude below a single small instance.

sensitivity.explanation: At 100% daily active, 3 sessions/day, 60 requests/session and a 20x peak factor the result is 4.2 requests/second. A single small managed instance handles that with roughly an order of magnitude of headroom, so the provisioning decision is identical at every point in the plausible range.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas in calculators/README.md; the Python calculator could not be executed in this environment.

results.formula: L = arrival_rate x service_time_seconds; provisioned = L / target_utilisation

safety_margin.rationale: Sized for 70% utilisation rather than 100%, because waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 1 (utilisation-and-queueing).

sensitivity.explanation: Even at the top of the plausible range (4.2 RPS peak, 120 ms service time) concurrency is 0.72, so a single process with a default pool of 4-8 workers is roughly 10x over-provisioned. Little's Law gives the mean; the worker floor absorbs the tail.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.

results.formula: concurrent = query_rate x query_time_seconds; pool_per_instance = max(min_pool, ceil(concurrent / instances x safety)); total = instances x pool_per_instance; pooler_justified = total > 0.8 x max_connections
results.calculation: concurrent = 1.4 x 0.005 = 0.0070; pool_per_instance = max(5, ceil(0.0070 x 4)) = 5; total = 1 x 5 = 5; 5 / 25 = 20% of max_connections, below the 80% threshold

safety_margin.rationale: 4x mean concurrency, because Little's Law gives the mean and a pool sized to the mean queues on connection acquisition during any burst. The floor of 5 dominates here anyway.

sensitivity.explanation: At 20 queries per request and 20 ms query time the demand is 0.11 concurrent connections, so the pool is still at the floor of 5 and still at 20% of max_connections. A connection pooler is not justified anywhere in the plausible range.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.

results.formula: bytes_per_day = writes_per_day x avg_record_bytes x index_overhead; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day x 365

safety_margin.rationale: index_overhead of 2.5 converts row size into stored size: indexes, tuple headers, page fill factor, and dead-tuple slack before vacuum.

sensitivity.explanation: Comments dominate row count but the total is 15 MB/year. Even 10x every write assumption gives 0.15 GB/year against a 10 GB starter plan, which is 67 years of runway. Database size is not a design constraint for this system.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.

assumptions.name: stored_bytes_per_photo
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear; the input to measure first

assumptions.name: index_overhead
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: none; object storage has no index or page overhead, so the 2.5 default does not apply

results.formula: bytes_per_day = writes_per_day x avg_record_bytes x index_overhead; bytes_per_year = bytes_per_day x 365
results.calculation: bytes_per_day = 6.8 x 3,500,000 x 1.0 = 2.38e7 = 24 MB/day; bytes_per_year = 24 MB x 365 = 8700 MB = 8.7 GB/year

safety_margin.rationale: The +40% derivative allowance already in stored_bytes_per_photo covers thumbnail and web-sized renditions. No further margin is applied because object storage is billed on actual bytes and grows without a plan limit.

sensitivity.explanation: Photo volume is the only storage figure worth measuring. Even at 10x (87 GB/year) the object-storage line is about GBP 1.30-2.20/month, so the architecture does not change; what changes is the egress bill, which is handled separately.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.
index_overhead deliberately set to 1.0: the 2.5 default is a relational-database concept and applying it to object storage would overstate the figure by 2.5x.

assumptions.name: avg_payload_bytes
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on egress and on the cost ceiling

results.formula: bytes_per_second = rps x avg_payload_bytes; egress_per_month = bytes_per_second x 2592000; cost = origin_gb x price_per_gb
results.calculation: bytes_per_second = 0.028 x 100000 = 2800 B/s; egress_per_month = 2800 x 2592000 = 7.26e9 B = 7.3 GB/month; cost = 7.3 x 0.065 = GBP 0.47/month

safety_margin.rationale: No margin applied: egress is billed on volume, so average RPS is the correct input and adding a peak margin would overstate the invoice by the peak factor.

sensitivity.explanation: 7.3 GB/month is two orders of magnitude below the ~1 TB/month threshold at which edge offload repays its complexity point (egress-cost). Even at the top of the range (55 GB/month) a CDN is not justified. Egress does, however, scale linearly with users and is the line that breaks the GBP 50 budget first: at about 3,800 users the total invoice reaches GBP 50 at mid-range prices.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.

results.formula: workers = ceil(arrival_rate x service_time_seconds / target_utilisation); capacity = workers / service_time_seconds
results.calculation: workers = ceil(0.000079 x 3 / 0.7) = ceil(0.00034) = 1; capacity = 1 / 3 = 0.33 jobs/second against an arrival rate of 0.000079 jobs/second, a margin of 4200x

safety_margin.rationale: Sized for 70% utilisation because queue depth grows without bound as utilisation approaches 1. The margin is irrelevant here: demand is 6.8 jobs/day.

sensitivity.explanation: At 1000x the assumed rate (6800 photos/day, 0.079 jobs/second) a single worker at 24% utilisation still keeps up. There is no queueing problem to solve, which is why image resizing stays in the request path rather than becoming a separate worker component.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.

assumptions.name: hours_per_point
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: linear on the operational line; judgement, not measurement

results.formula: infrastructure = sum(quantity x unit_price); operational = complexity_points x hours_per_point x loaded_hourly_rate; total = infrastructure + operational
results.calculation: infrastructure_low = 5 + 10 + (8.7 x 0.015 = 0.13) + (7.3 x 0.04 = 0.29) + 0.02 backup + 0 error tracking (free tier) = GBP 15.44; infrastructure_high = 15 + 20 + (8.7 x 0.025 = 0.22) + (7.3 x 0.09 = 0.66) + 0.05 + 0 = GBP 35.93; operational = 4 x 4 x 60 = GBP 960; total = GBP 975 to GBP 996

safety_margin.rationale: No margin applied to the invoice: the price table already gives ranges, and the high end of the range is the conservative figure. The GBP 50 constraint is met with roughly GBP 14-35 of headroom.

sensitivity.explanation: The infrastructure line is GBP 15-36 and the operational line is GBP 480-1440 (at 2-6 hours/point). The operational term dominates by a factor of about 30, which is why the complexity budget rather than the GBP 50 budget is the binding constraint on this design. The GBP 50 budget only binds on growth: it is exceeded at roughly 1,700-8,300 registered users depending on where prices fall in their ranges, centre about 3,800.

notes: Computed from the documented formulas; calculator not executable in this environment.
Prices from knowledge/cost/_pricing.md, checked 2026-08-09. Indicative, provider-neutral, not quotes.
hours_per_point = 4 and loaded_hourly_rate = 60 are judgement constants, not measurements (operational-cost-model).

components.name: Application runtime (single deployed unit, managed platform)
components.justification: Peak 0.28 requests/second and mean concurrency 0.048 (Little's Law). One small managed instance is roughly three orders of magnitude over-provisioned, so horizontal scaling and a load balancer have no measured problem to solve. Image resizing runs in-request in this same process at 6.8 photos/day.

components.name: Relational database (managed, smallest class)
components.justification: The workload is relational: recipes belong to authors, comments belong to recipes and authors, tags are many-to-many. Growth is 0.015 GB/year against a 10 GB starter plan, and peak query rate is 1.4/second at 5 connections against a limit of 25. Full-text search over roughly 600 recipes/year is served by a GIN index on the same instance.

components.name: Object storage (managed)
components.justification: Photos are 8.7 GB/year against 0.015 GB/year of relational data, a ratio of about 580:1. Serving 3.5 MB/photo from application instances or a database would put the largest byte volume in the least durable and most expensive place; object storage costs about GBP 0.13-0.22/month at this volume and gives durability the team does not have to operate.

components.name: Managed error tracking (free tier)
components.justification: Two developers with no operations capacity and no availability target need to learn about a broken deploy from a tool rather than from a user. At about 2,400 requests/day the event volume sits inside every free tier, so the infrastructure cost is GBP 0 and the cost is entirely the fourth complexity point. This is the one stage-2 element deliberately pulled forward; dropping it returns the design to 3/4.

rejected_components.reason: Peak read rate is 1.3 queries/second against a database that is comfortable, and no single key approaches the ~10 requests/second threshold in when-not-to-cache. A cache here would add a component, a staleness class and an invalidation question on every write path in exchange for relieving load the origin does not notice. In-process caching of rendered fragments is available at 0 points if needed.
rejected_components.revisit_when: One identified query exceeds 100 requests/minute at over 50 ms, measured before anything is added; or database CPU exceeds 70% sustained over 3 days and query optimisation has already been attempted.

rejected_components.reason: Origin egress is 7.3 GB/month. egress-cost puts the break-even for a CDN's complexity point at roughly 1 TB/month, and states that below a few hundred GB/month the saving does not repay the component. The saving at present is under GBP 0.70/month against 1 complexity point worth about GBP 240/month of engineering attention. If the object store or application platform includes edge delivery at no extra operational surface, take it: it costs 0 points and the arithmetic above does not apply.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Origin egress exceeds 250 GB/month for 2 consecutive months, read from the provider billing dashboard. This is the trigger most likely to fire first, because egress scales linearly with users and is what breaks the GBP 50 budget at roughly 3,800 users.

rejected_components.reason: Image processing demand is 6.8 jobs/day (0.000079 jobs/second) against a single worker's capacity of 0.33 jobs/second, a margin of 4200x. when-you-need-streaming applies only at stages 4-5 and is not remotely in range. When asynchrony is eventually needed the first move is a database-backed job queue on the database already running, which costs 0 complexity points, not a broker.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Image uploads exceed 200/day, or p95 upload latency exceeds 5 seconds twice in a week. The action is a database-backed queue in the existing database, not a broker; a broker needs sustained throughput that the database-backed queue cannot carry, which is orders of magnitude above this.

rejected_components.kind: separate worker service / independently deployed service
rejected_components.reason: Each additional independently deployed service costs 1 point against a budget already at 4/4, and buys nothing at 6.8 background jobs/day. Resizing in the request path costs 0 points and 3 seconds of a request that happens seven times a day.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Background work exceeds a single process's capacity at 70% utilisation, or in-request work pushes p95 upload latency over 5 seconds.

rejected_components.reason: read-replicas applies at stages 3-5. The primary is serving 1.4 queries/second and a replica would introduce replication lag, which makes read-after-write a correctness problem on the comment and publish paths in exchange for offloading load the primary does not feel.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Database CPU exceeds 70% sustained over 3 days AND the workload is measured to be read-dominated AND query optimisation and indexing have already been exhausted.

rejected_components.reason: Recipe search is the plausible reason to reach for one, but the corpus is about 600 recipes/year. PostgreSQL full-text search with a GIN index over tens of thousands of rows returns in single-digit milliseconds. A search cluster is a second datastore technology (+1 point on top of its own cost) against a budget with no headroom.
rejected_components.revisit_when: The corpus exceeds 100,000 recipes, or p95 search latency exceeds 300 ms with a GIN index confirmed to be in use by EXPLAIN.

rejected_components.reason: Demand is 5 connections (the pool floor) against an assumed limit of 25, which is 20% and well below the 80% threshold at which connection-pooling says a pooler is justified. Below that threshold it adds a hop and a process for nothing.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Connection utilisation exceeds 80% of max_connections for 1 hour, recurring. This is also the reason serverless compute was rejected: it inverts this arithmetic and forces the pooler.

rejected_components.reason: 4 complexity points, which is the entire budget for this team, to schedule one container serving 0.28 requests/second. Rule R-F also blocks it: this is a stage-1 system and self-managed orchestration is stage-4 machinery.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Not at this scale. Re-evaluate only above roughly 10 independently deployed services with genuine per-service scaling requirements, and only with dedicated operations headcount, which raises the budget by 4 points per person.

rejected_components.reason: relational-vs-document selects on workload, not preference. Recipes have stable structure and heavy relationships: author, comments, tags, likes, all of which are joins. There is no heterogeneous-schema or embedded-aggregate pressure here.
rejected_components.revisit_when: Recipe documents become genuinely heterogeneous per user AND queries stop joining across entities. Neither is on the roadmap described.

rejected_components.reason: No availability target was stated, and availability-targets says not to invent one. A multi-AZ replicated database is GBP 400-600/month against a GBP 50 budget, so it is 8-12x the entire infrastructure allowance to buy availability nobody has asked for.
rejected_components.revisit_when: The business states an availability target of 99.95% or better and raises the infrastructure budget accordingly. This is a requirements change, not a metric.

rejected_components.reason: Log ingestion is priced at GBP 0.40-2.00 per GB and observability-cost identifies it as the classic unbudgeted line. The managed platform's own logs and metrics dashboards cover every trigger in this design at 0 additional points, and error tracking covers the exception path.
rejected_components.revisit_when: A production incident cannot be diagnosed from platform logs and error-tracker events within the team's tolerance, twice in a quarter.

options.description: Single application codebase deployed as one unit on a managed platform, with a managed relational database, managed object storage for photos, in-request image resizing, and free-tier managed error tracking. Photos are uploaded through the app, resized in-process, written to object storage, and served to browsers directly from object-storage URLs.
trade_offs: Availability is roughly 99%: a single application instance and a single-AZ database mean planned deploys and database maintenance are visible to users, and recovery from database loss is a restore measured in tens of minutes.
Image resizing in the request path occupies an application worker for about 3 seconds per photo. Harmless at 6.8 photos/day; the first thing that breaks if uploads become popular.
The complexity budget is fully spent at 4/4, so the next component requires removing one of these four or adding an engineer.
The GBP 50 infrastructure budget is met with headroom now but scales out at roughly 3,800 registered users, driven by egress rather than compute.
Managed services cost more on the invoice than self-hosting the same things, which is the correct trade for a two-person team but is a real cash cost.

options.description: Identical to option A with the managed error tracker removed, leaving application runtime, relational database and object storage. This is the strictly simplest viable architecture for the stated requirements.
options.reason: Genuinely viable and it preserves a point of headroom, which has real value for a team with none. It is deferred rather than selected because two developers with no operations capacity and no availability target need a tool that tells them a deploy broke, and the alternative is finding out from a user. If the team would rather hold the fourth point in reserve for a future requirement, this option is the correct one and nothing else in the design changes. The measurement that decides it: whether platform logs alone surface production exceptions within the team's tolerance over one month of real traffic.
trade_offs: One point of headroom preserved, which is the capacity to absorb one future requirement without a rethink.
Production exceptions are discovered by reading platform logs, which in practice means discovering them when a user reports them.
Same infrastructure cost as option A, since the error tracker is free at this volume: the trade is entirely operational surface against diagnostic speed.

options.description: One small virtual machine running the application behind a self-managed reverse proxy, with PostgreSQL installed on the same box and photos on local block storage. The cheapest possible invoice.
options.reason: Rejected on the operational-cost-model arithmetic, not on taste. Self-hosted stateless (2) plus self-hosted stateful (3) is 5 points against a budget of 4, and 5 points is about GBP 1,200/month of engineering attention against option A's GBP 960, to save roughly GBP 5-10/month on the invoice. It also puts 8.7 GB/year of user photos on a single unreplicated disk whose backup is the team's problem. The measurement that changes the answer: if the team already operates PostgreSQL on virtual machines for another system, the marginal points fall to roughly 1-2 and this becomes the cheaper architecture on both lines; or if managed database pricing for this workload exceeded about GBP 300/month, at which point the invoice difference would outrun the operational difference.
trade_offs: Cheapest invoice by GBP 5-10/month, and the free-tier and per-GB pricing traps of managed services do not apply.
Everything is in one place, which is genuinely simpler to reason about until it is not.
Backups, patching, PostgreSQL upgrades, disk growth and failover are all the team's responsibility, and an untested restore is not a backup.
Photos on local disk are a single point of permanent data loss, which is the one failure this product cannot recover from.

options.description: Serverless functions for the application, a managed relational database behind a connection pooler, managed object storage with presigned direct upload, a CDN in front of images, and a queue for out-of-band resizing.
options.reason: 50% over a budget of 4, and the excess buys nothing measurable: the CDN offloads 7.3 GB/month against a 1 TB/month break-even, the queue handles 6.8 jobs/day, and the pooler exists only to repair a problem serverless itself creates. On invoice it is competitive — 72,000 invocations/month is about GBP 0.04 — so the rejection is on operational surface and on the fact that image resizing runs into function time and memory limits. The measurement that changes the answer: if the application instance line exceeded about GBP 25/month while median CPU utilisation stayed under 5%, idle compute would be the dominant waste and per-invocation pricing would win.
trade_offs: Compute cost tracks usage almost exactly, which suits a workload that is idle 99.99% of the time.
No instance to patch or size.
Six components and three of them exist to compensate for the first one; cold starts on a low-traffic app are user-visible on the first request after an idle period.
Local development and debugging are materially harder for a two-person team, which is a velocity cost at stage 1.

availability.achievable: ~99% (about 7.3 hours of permitted downtime per month)
availability.explanation: No target was stated and availability-targets says not to invent one. What this architecture actually delivers is roughly 99%: a single application instance with platform-level process restart, a single-AZ managed database with automated daily backups and point-in-time recovery, and object storage whose durability is the provider's problem. The binding constraint is database recovery: restoring from backup is tens of minutes to hours with a human in the loop, so any target implying less than about an hour of monthly downtime is not deliverable here. 99.9% would require deploys without extended downtime, automated restart and a tested restore procedure, all of which are achievable at 0 additional complexity points and are recommended. 99.95% requires database failover, which means a multi-AZ replicated database at GBP 400-600/month against a GBP 50 budget, and is therefore a budget conversation rather than an architecture one.

triggers.source: cloud provider billing dashboard, reviewed at month end
triggers.action: Break the invoice down by line and re-run the bandwidth and storage calculations against measured volumes. Egress is the expected dominant line; evaluate edge offload against its current price before adding compute.
triggers.owner: the two developers, at the monthly billing review
triggers.notes: 120% of the stated GBP 50 budget. Capacity analysis puts the crossover at roughly 1,700-8,300 registered users depending on where provider prices fall, centred on about 3,800.

triggers.source: cloud provider billing dashboard, data transfer line
triggers.action: Compute the cost of edge offload against current origin egress pricing and current measured image payload sizes. Reducing served image dimensions is often the larger win than adding a CDN and costs 0 complexity points.
triggers.owner: the two developers, at the monthly billing review
triggers.notes: Present volume is 7.3 GB/month. 250 GB is set well below the ~1 TB/month break-even in egress-cost so that the analysis starts with runway rather than after the invoice arrives.

triggers.source: application admin page, checked at the monthly product review
triggers.action: Re-run the full capacity analysis with measured daily-active share, requests per session and photo sizes rather than the assumed values in this design.
triggers.owner: the two developers, at the monthly product review
triggers.notes: This is the sensitivity limit from the cost analysis, not a round number. Compute holds to roughly 10,000 users; the GBP 50 budget is what breaks first, at about 3,800.

triggers.metric: application instance CPU utilisation at peak
triggers.action: Profile the dominant request path and confirm whether in-request image resizing is the cause before changing instance size or count. Latency is still linear at 70%, so there is time to analyse.
Identify the dominant query from the database's own statistics view; evaluate indexing and query optimisation before considering a replica or a cache.

triggers.metric: database storage used as a share of the plan limit
triggers.action: Identify what is growing against the projected 0.015 GB/year and decide retention or plan size then, not at 95%.
triggers.notes: 60% of a 10 GB starter plan is 6 GB. At the projected growth rate this should not fire for decades, so if it fires the projection is wrong and that is the finding.

triggers.metric: active database connections as a share of max_connections
triggers.window: sustained over 1 hour, recurring within a month
triggers.action: Re-run the connections calculation against the measured query rate and query time; evaluate pool configuration before adding a connection pooler as a component.
triggers.notes: 80% of max_connections is the threshold at which connection-pooling says a pooler becomes justified. Present demand is 20%.

triggers.metric: p95 end-to-end latency of the photo upload endpoint
triggers.source: application request timing, emitted to the managed platform metrics dashboard
triggers.action: Profile the resize step and evaluate moving it to a database-backed job queue on the existing database, which costs 0 complexity points, before considering a separate worker service or a broker.
triggers.notes: This metric does not exist yet. Instrumenting per-endpoint request timing on the upload and search paths is a prerequisite of this decision, not a follow-up, because in-request resizing is the design choice this trigger guards.

triggers.metric: p95 latency of the recipe search query
triggers.source: application request timing on the search endpoint, plus the database statement statistics view
triggers.action: Confirm with EXPLAIN that the GIN full-text index is in use; if it is, re-run the analysis for search against measured corpus size before evaluating a dedicated search component.
triggers.notes: Requires the same request-timing instrumentation as upload-p95-latency.

triggers.metric: days since the last successful restore of a production backup into a scratch database
triggers.source: a dated line in the team's operations note, checked at the quarterly review
triggers.action: Perform a restore into a scratch database, time it, and record the measured recovery time. If it exceeds the tolerance the business turns out to have, that is a requirements conversation about the availability target.
triggers.owner: the two developers, at the quarterly review
triggers.notes: An untested restore is not a backup (backup-restore-and-pitr). Database recovery time is the binding constraint on this design's availability, and it is currently unmeasured.

open_questions: What is the actual average photo size and photos-per-recipe? This is the dominant uncertain input in the whole analysis: it drives object storage, egress, and therefore the point at which the GBP 50 budget is exceeded. One week of measurement resolves it.

Is there an availability expectation nobody has written down? The design delivers about 99% and recovers from database loss by restore. If a day of downtime would be a business problem, that is a requirements change with a cost attached.

Are the users in the UK or EU? No compliance requirements were stated, but consumer accounts plus user-uploaded photos carry baseline data-protection duties regardless: account deletion that actually removes photos from object storage, and a stated retention policy. Both are cheap to build now and expensive to retrofit.

Is user-uploaded content moderated? Public photo upload with no review is a product and legal exposure rather than an architectural one, but it changes whether an upload needs a pending state before publication.

Has either developer operated a managed relational database and managed object storage before? If not, the unfamiliar-technology modifier adds 1-2 points and this design goes over budget, which would make option A0 the correct selection instead.
